items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I’m going to lyricize and sing the Miles Davis “‘Round About Midnight” album. Yeah. That’s going to be a labor of love. I love that album.

ctx.x: What a wonderful — What’s in the immediate future for you? European tour?

Well I’m going on this tour. I’m getting together another album and I’m going to do a vocalese project. I’m going to lyricize and sing the Miles Davis “‘Round About Midnight” album. Yeah. That’s going to be a labor of love. I love that album. I think it’s the best jazz album I’ve heard since Bird and Diz.
Do you work at the piano when you do this?

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Miles knew me, Dizzy knew me, all the cats knew me.

ctx.x: With this long goatee. That’s the way Gerry had this long, red beard and a shock of red hair. And jeans, no socks and tennis shoes. That was how he was dressed on the bandstand. Well those guys were spending all their money on heroin. They were shooting up all day every day. And he was living uptown with Bird at that time. And Roy Haynes was on drums, Curly Russell was on bass, and Bud Powell was on piano. So they were playing “The Song Is You,” the song that I scatted with him as I went by. And as I © Hamilton…

walked past the bandstand, now it had been two years and four months since I had seen him for about nine minutes on this bandstand in Toledo, which is the heart of nowhere. And as I walked past the bandstand, he’s playing [scats], “hey Jon, how you doin’ man, you want to sing some?” I almost fainted. It took my breath away. I said good Lord, who the hell is that? I couldn’t believe that. And after the set he came over to my table, sat down, talked to me and just said, “what you doing?” And I said, “well I just…

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He moved me over, took the fork and knife out of my hands, and ate my steak. I said, “You ate my steak.”

ctx.x: On Move. Yeah, I think she did. And I think that needed some correction. I think if Miles had paid any attention to it, he might have been angry too. At that time he wasn’t listening to any more jazz anyway. So we escaped him. Because when Annie did his solo on Four, I was eating a steak up in Toronto. He moved me over, took the fork and knife out of my hands, and ate my steak. I said, “You ate my steak.” He said, “You mess with my solos, I’ll mess with your food.” And mess wasn’t the word. But these guys are…
Yeah. What is it? One of the quotations that said that not only do you sing the solos, but sometimes you outdo the originals. I think that’s fantastic.
